rv.q: Michael Grandage’s robustly elegant production guides us confidently through Raicek’s appealingly murky mixture of sex, power and professional status.
Still, this relatable humour sits increasingly uncomfortably inside the oddly shaped outlines of Ibsen’s play.
There are moments of great intensity, mostly in the scenes featuring Fleetwood, and real candescence to the writing at its best.
Ultimately Raicek has created as many problems as she’s solved in trying to ‘fix’ the original story.
Instead of busting free of the original, the chic, effortful result proves an intriguing but frustrating half-way house.
But none of it gels. Blazing recriminations are interspersed with clotted dialogue that's achingly right-on.
It is a puzzle that Michael Grandage, fleetest of directors, was drawn to this script, which makes actors shrivel.
This contemporary renovation looks fabulous, but you long for the rich strangeness of the original.
This new piece feels like one of those renovations that hasn’t quite worked.
But the dialogue is so carefully manicured that there’s an inescapable sense of effort and contrivance.
But really, it’s a load of old nonsense.
Unfortunately, her characters express themselves in sophomoric dialogue in which every other sentence tries to express some grand philosophical truth.
Now, a sharp exploration of women and empowerment, My Master Builder, in its comedy and drive, is an exhilarating show.
Dramatically, this is pure gold.
It feels too contrived to be moving.

He is about to unveil the reimagined whaling chapel which a decade earlier, burned with his young son Max inside. The glass edifice which he straddles to make a speech (despite issues with vertigo) is designed to be a star shafted portal to the celestial afterlife!

My Master Builder is seductive to the eye throughout, but for a play steeped in second chances and the notion of returning, metaphorically speaking, to the emotional well, this study in "the tragic wreckage of the past" exerts insufficient hold over the present.
The real problem with the play is that it’s all a bit dull and grandiose and Grandage’s direction is a bit flabby – too much tell and not enough show.
As the evening progresses, it becomes so weird and distancing that it is hard to care about its outcome.

Raicek and Grandage’s efforts to bring to light the strain people put on one another, and the ways in which we can find ourselves as pawns in someone else’s unending chess game, have certainly succeeded.
Kate Fleetwood’s Elena is perhaps the most memorable, delivering a performance that is both chilling and compelling.
The play’s at its best at at its fieriest, some of the late rows between Henry and Elena reaching almost Who’s-afraid-of-Virginia-Woolf levels.
The cast do well with what they’ve got to work with.

That Ibsen’s name isn’t on the poster is a telling sign. That in some ways is a good thing: probably Ibsen’s most autobiographical play, it tells the story of an older man in a failing marriage who comes into contact after a decade with a much younger woman he had once fallen in love with.
The effect is both horrifying and thrilling. It's like watching a controlled collapse – precise, devastating, and impossible to look away from.
My Master Builder is an elegant construction well worth inhabiting.

cn.t: McGregor's return after 17 years draws mixed reviews for this Ibsen-inspired drama. Critics praise Fleetwood's fierce performance and the feminist reimagining, but many find Raicek's debut script pretentious and question whether it justifies existing.
